summary:
Southeast Sulawesi stands under the national framework of Indonesia, which is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national morality provisions. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors; in Aceh two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. Southeast Sulawesi is not among the provinces reported as having its own criminalising regulation.

Physical risk is rising nationally. Vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people, and reporting in August 2026 ties the surge to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 listing LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism, placing them inside national defence policy.

Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him; Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment. In March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words including Grindr, and a bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Documents are restrictive. Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, and no national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Within Southeast Sulawesi itself, the source inventory records no enforcement incident, raid or local regulation directed at same-sex relationships or transgender people. Research on the provincial capital, Kendari, describes same-sex communities living discreetly and reports no provincial-level criminalising measure.
tangentialFactors:
OutRight Action International's 2022 report, 'Creeping Criminalisation: Mapping of Indonesia's National Laws and Regional Regulations That Violate Human Rights of Women and LGBTIQ People', examines discriminatory national laws and regional regulations in eight focus provinces: Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta. Southeast Sulawesi is not among them; the Sulawesi entry in that set is South Sulawesi.

The same report finds substantial overlap between those provinces alongside significant regional variation in dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear, and states that its findings apply to regions beyond the focus set. Southeast Sulawesi therefore sits in a national environment where sub-national regulation of gender expression is documented, even though no such regulation for this province appears in the inventory.

The national provisions that a visitor in Southeast Sulawesi is most likely to encounter are the penal code provisions in force since 2 January 2026 and the 2006 pornography statute, both of which apply throughout Indonesia rather than only in the provinces with their own criminalising rules.
localsOnly:
A qualitative study by Universitas Halu Oleo researchers, published in Jurnal Budaya Etnika Vol. 8 No. 2 on 23 December 2024, describes gay life in Kendari, the capital of Southeast Sulawesi. Gay groups in the city say same-sex orientation has partly been converted into an economically valued 'profession', and that after identifying as gay they become more introverted and careful about expressing their feelings to others.

Same-sex communities in Kendari live discreetly, and the article reports no enforcement incident, raid or local regulation affecting them in the province.

Legal gender recognition for residents follows the national requirement of sex reassignment surgery plus a judge's approval, with no third-gender or X marker available on documents. Because no national non-discrimination statute covers gender identity or sexual orientation, residents who are harassed or dismissed have no statutory claim to protection.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the inventory contains no province-level regulation of Southeast Sulawesi addressing same-sex conduct, dress codes, curfews or the presence of transgender people, and no reporting of police or vigilante action against LGBT people in the province. Whether such a regulation exists and is simply unsourced cannot be determined from the material reviewed.

Unresolved: whether the extra-marital sex provisions of the penal code in force since 2 January 2026 have been applied in Southeast Sulawesi is not sourced; national reporting characterises prosecutions as selective rather than systematic but does not break down by province.

Unresolved: OutRight Action International's 2022 mapping did not examine Southeast Sulawesi, so the regional-variation findings for dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear rest on other provinces and are indicative rather than documented for this one.

Not sourced: the inventory records no hate-crime statistics, no data on availability of gender-affirming medical care, and no information on entry or border screening practice at Southeast Sulawesi's points of entry.
